role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (systematic review of 703 papers)
quote: Bar graphs were the most commonly used figures for presenting continuous data. 85.6% of papers included at least one bar graph.
problem: Continuous data from small samples shown as bar graphs that hide the distribution
need: Default graph for continuous group data should show every point (dot/box/violin) rather than a bar of the mean

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (systematic review of 703 papers)
quote: Most of these papers used bar graphs that showed mean ± SE (77.6%, Panel B in S2 Fig ), rather than mean ± SD (15.3%).
problem: Error bars default to SEM, which looks smaller and does not describe variability
need: Make SD (or the raw points) the default for describing spread and require an explicit, labelled choice of SEM/CI

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (systematic review of 703 papers)
quote: Figures that provide detailed information about the distribution of the data were seldom used. 13.4% of articles included at least one univariate scatterplot, 5.3% included at least one box plot, and 8.0% included at least one histogram.
problem: Distribution-revealing plots (scatter, box, histogram) are rarely used
need: Offer dot plots, box plots and histograms as first-class one-click graph types for column data

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: In 75% of the papers that we reviewed, the minimum sample size for any group shown in a figure was between two and six. Univariate scatterplots are the best choice for showing the distribution of the data in these small samples, as boxplots and histograms would be difficult to interpret.
problem: Summary-statistic graphics are used on groups of 2-6 observations where summaries are not meaningful
need: Detect small n per group and steer to univariate scatterplots showing every point instead of bars, box plots or histograms

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: 78.1% of studies performed only parametric analyses. 13.6% of studies used both parametric and nonparametric analyses, whereas 3.8% included only nonparametric analyses.
problem: Parametric tests are applied by default to small samples whose distribution cannot be assessed
need: Show the data next to the test, check assumptions, and offer a nonparametric or transformed alternative when n is too small to judge normality

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (328 papers audited)
quote: However, papers in our sample were routinely missing essential information about both types of tests: 213 papers (95% of the papers that used ANOVA) did not contain the information needed to determine what type of ANOVA was performed, and 26.7% of papers did not specify what post-hoc test was performed.
problem: Methods sections do not say which ANOVA (factors, repeated measures) or which post-hoc test was run
need: Auto-generate a complete methods paragraph naming the ANOVA type, factors, between/within status and post-hoc test

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (328 papers audited)
quote: Among papers that used one-way ANOVAs, 60.9% (67/110) used a one-way ANOVA for an analysis where the study design included two or more factors.
problem: One-way ANOVA used when the design has two or more factors
need: Design-first test chooser that asks how many factors define the groups and steers multi-factor designs to two-way ANOVA

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (328 papers audited)
quote: Our data suggest that scientists should be cautious about this assumption, as 28.3% of papers that did not indicate that repeated measures were used (52/184) included at least one ANOVA that appeared to require repeated measures.
problem: Repeated-measures structure ignored or unreported in ANOVA
need: Ask whether the same subjects were measured repeatedly and default to RM/mixed analysis when they were

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: Over half of the papers (53%; 95/179) did not specify whether any t-tests were paired or unpaired
problem: Whether a t-test was paired or unpaired is not reported (and 'Student's t-test' is used ambiguously)
need: Name the exact test variant (paired/unpaired, Welch/equal variance) in every output and exported legend

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (328 papers audited)
quote: Among the studies in our sample that included ANOVA ( Figure 8 ), more than 95% failed to report the F-statistic or degrees of freedom.
problem: F statistic and degrees of freedom omitted, so results cannot be verified
need: Export results with test statistic, df and exact P in a ready-to-paste reporting line

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (328 papers audited)
quote: Moreover, 79.7% of the papers that included t-tests reported ranges of p-values instead of exact p-values.
problem: P values reported as thresholds (p<0.05) instead of exact values
need: Report exact P values by default in result tables, graphs and methods text

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology (328 papers audited)
quote: This is problematic because it is possible to complete a PhD without being trained in statistics: only 67.5% of the top NIH-funded physiology departments in the United States required statistics training for some or all PhD programs that the department participated in ( Weissgerber et al., 2016a ).
problem: Many bench scientists have no formal statistics training
need: Tool must teach in context (explain why a test was chosen) rather than assume statistical expertise

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology / data visualization
quote: The common practice of displaying summary statistics can be misleading, as many different data distributions can lead to the same graph ( Fig 2 ) [ 1 ].
problem: Line graphs of mean ± error hide individual trajectories and distributions in repeated-measures data
need: For paired/longitudinal data, offer spaghetti plots or individual-change views alongside the summary line

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology / data visualization
quote: Outliers are common in such small datasets, and it is difficult to determine the distribution of the data.
problem: In small datasets outliers drive the mean and the distribution cannot be judged from summaries
need: Show raw points and let users toggle summaries (mean/median, SD/IQR) so outliers stay visible

role: peer-reviewed critique, peripheral vascular disease (206 papers audited)
quote: Table 1: Correcting Common Visualization Problems in Peripheral Vascular Disease Journals Replace bar graphs with figures that show the data distribution: 47.7% of papers used bar graphs to present continuous data, typically for small datasets.
problem: Bar graphs still used for continuous small-sample data
need: Make dot/box/violin plots the default for continuous column data

role: peer-reviewed critique, peripheral vascular disease (206 papers audited)
quote: Use symmetric jittering in dot plots to make all data points visible: Among papers with dot plots (n = 39), 46.2% included overlapping data points that were not clearly visible.
problem: Dot plots with overlapping, hidden points
need: Dot plots should jitter/beeswarm symmetrically by default so every point is visible

role: peer-reviewed critique, peripheral vascular disease (206 papers audited)
quote: Use semi-transparency or show gradients to make overlapping points visible in scatterplots and flow-cytometry figures: Scatterplots in 89.2% of papers (33/37) had overlapping points, however only 12.1% of papers (4/33) used techniques like semi-transparency, shaded color gradients, or gradient lines to make overlapping points visible.
problem: Overplotted scatterplots hide data density
need: Provide point transparency / density shading options for dense XY and cytometry scatterplots

role: peer-reviewed critique, peripheral vascular disease (206 papers audited)
quote: While 12.6% of papers (26/206) used a color map on a graph or clinical image, only 15.4% of these papers (4/26) used color maps in which key features were visible to someone with deuteranopia.
problem: Colour maps unreadable to colour-blind readers
need: Default to colour-blind-safe palettes and offer a deuteranopia preview

role: peer-reviewed critique, peripheral vascular disease (206 papers audited)
quote: Most papers with heat maps used color palettes that were not color blind safe (7/12, 58.3%).
problem: Heat maps use red-green or other non-CVD-safe palettes
need: Heat-map palettes should be perceptually uniform and colour-blind safe by default

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (206 papers) and primer, vascular biology
quote: Very small samples do not provide enough data to distinguish between normal, skewed or bimodal distributions ( ... Normality tests are underpowered when n is small and often fail to detect non-normal distributions.
problem: Normality tests on tiny samples are used to justify parametric tests
need: Warn that a 'passed' normality test at small n is uninformative; base the choice on design/prior knowledge and show the data

role: peer-reviewed critique, peripheral vascular disease (206 papers audited)
quote: In most bar graphs in our sample, error bars show the standard error (66.3%) rather than the standard deviation (20.9%) or 95% confidence interval (2.3%).
problem: SEM error bars dominate
need: Default error bars to SD or 95% CI with an explicit legend statement

role: peer-reviewed critique, peripheral vascular disease (206 papers audited)
quote: As the y-axis typically starts at zero and ends above the highest error bar, bars often include biologically impossible values (Zone of Irrelevance, Figure 1 ) while omitting high values that were observed in the sample (Zone of Invisibility).
problem: Bar height and axis range distort the perceived data range
need: Choose axis ranges from the data distribution, not from bar heights, and show observed extremes

role: peer-reviewed critique, biochemistry / data visualization
quote: Clusters of non-independent data, such as technical replicates or mice from the same litter, are common in basic science research, yet these data are often inappropriately analyzed ( 32 ).
problem: Clustered data (technical replicates, littermates) analysed as independent
need: Let users mark the cluster (experiment, litter, animal) for each point, colour by cluster and analyse at the right level

role: peer-reviewed critique, biochemistry / data visualization
quote: Information about the presence and type of clustering is rarely apparent in static graphics but can be easily visualized and explored using the interactive dotplot tool.
problem: Static graphs hide which points belong together
need: Graphs should encode the cluster/replicate of each point (colour or symbol) so readers can see the structure

role: peer-reviewed critique, meta-research across 23 biomedical fields
quote: Bar graphs are more often used incorrectly to display continuous data than they are used correctly to display counts or proportions.
problem: Bar graphs of continuous data persist a decade after critiques
need: Steer users away from bar graphs for continuous replicates at graph-creation time (bars only for counts/proportions)

role: peer-reviewed critique, meta-research across 23 biomedical fields
quote: The proportion of papers that use bar graphs of continuous data varies markedly across fields (range in 2020: 4–58%), with high rates in biochemistry and cell biology, complementary and alternative medicine, physiology, genetics, oncology and carcinogenesis, pharmacology, microbiology and immunology.
problem: Bench fields (cell biology, pharmacology, immunology) have the highest rates of bar graphs of continuous data
need: Bench-oriented tool defaults matter most: dot/box/violin as default for these users

role: peer-reviewed critique, meta-research across 23 biomedical fields
quote: Fewer than 25% of papers use flow charts, which provide information about attrition and the risk of bias.
problem: Sample attrition/exclusions not shown
need: Track excluded values/animals and produce an attrition summary for the report

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell biology
quote: The resulting P values are worse than useless: counting each cell as a separate n can easily result in false-positive rates of >50% ( Aarts et al., 2015 ).
problem: Each cell counted as n, inflating significance
need: Require the user to identify biological replicates and compute the test on replicate means (or a mixed model), not on cells

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell biology
quote: However, calculating standard error of the mean by inputting data from all cells individually fails in two ways: first, the natural variability we expect from biology would be better summarized with a descriptive measure, like standard deviation; and second, the inflated n produces error bars that are artificially small (due to √ n in the denominator) and do not communicate the repeatability of the experiment.
problem: SEM computed over all cells gives tiny, meaningless error bars
need: Compute error bars from replicate-level means and label which n they use

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell biology
quote: To correct that, “SuperPlots” superimpose summary statistics from biological replicates consisting of independent experiments on top of data from all cells, and P values were calculated using an n of three, not 300.
problem: Plots do not show both cell-level spread and replicate-level reproducibility
need: Built-in SuperPlot graph type: cells as small dots coloured by replicate, replicate means overlaid, stats on replicate means

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell biology
quote: For example, if you have three biological replicates of control and treated samples, and you measure the cell diameter of 200 cells in each sample, first calculate the mean of those 200 measurements for each sample, then run a t test on those sample means (three control, three treated).
problem: Users do not know how to aggregate cell-level data before testing
need: One-step 'aggregate by replicate then test' workflow from a long-format table

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience
quote: 12% of papers had pseudoreplication and a further 36% were suspected of having pseudoreplication, but it was not possible to determine for certain because insufficient information was provided.
problem: Pseudoreplication (non-independent observations treated as independent)
need: Capture the experimental structure (animal/cell/slice) and refuse to treat sub-samples as independent n without warning

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience
quote: Conclusions Pseudoreplication can undermine the conclusions of a statistical analysis, and it would be easier to detect if the sample size, degrees of freedom, the test statistic, and precise p -values are reported.
problem: Missing df/test statistic hide pseudoreplication from reviewers
need: Always output n, df, test statistic and exact P together so the unit of analysis can be audited

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience
quote: The change in p -value between the two analyses is six orders of magnitude, which demonstrates the importance of dealing with pseudoreplication appropriately.
problem: Analysing 20 within-rat measurements as independent gives P=2.7e-7 instead of 0.287
need: Average sub-samples per experimental unit (or fit a mixed model) automatically when a grouping column is given

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience
quote: The terms sample , replicate , observation , experimental unit , n , and experiment have overlapping meanings, are often used interchangeably, and can have different meanings based on the context.
problem: Ambiguous vocabulary about replicates and n
need: Use explicit, defined terms (experimental unit vs technical replicate) in the UI and in the generated methods

role: peer-reviewed critique, animal and cell-culture research (200 papers audited)
quote: Nearly half of the studies (46%, 95% CI = 38%–53%) had pseudoreplication while 32% (95% CI = 26%–39%) provided insufficient information to make a judgement.
problem: Pseudoreplication in prenatal/litter studies
need: Design wizard that asks what was randomised to treatment (the experimental unit) and sets N accordingly

role: peer-reviewed critique, animal and cell-culture research (200 papers audited)
quote: First, we argue that the frequent and common distinction made between ‘biological’ and ‘technical’ replication is unhelpful because they are inconsistently defined, do not capture the important characteristics of an experiment, and do not clarify what to replicate.
problem: Biological vs technical replicate labels do not tell users what N is
need: Define N via the experimental unit (entity randomly assigned to intervention), not via replicate labels

role: peer-reviewed critique, animal and cell-culture research (200 papers audited)
quote: Confusing pseudoreplication for genuine replication artificially inflates the sample size, thereby inflating the apparent evidence supporting a scientific claim, and contributes to irreproducible results.
problem: Inflated n gives false positives
need: Flag when the analysed n exceeds the number of independent units entered

role: peer-reviewed critique, animal and cell-culture research (200 papers audited)
quote: The wrong choice of replicate cannot be fixed by a clever statistical analysis after the experiment is completed (e.g., using multilevel or hierarchical models); it needs to be planned at the design stage.
problem: Replication planned wrongly before the experiment
need: Planning tool (before data collection) that maps the design to the experimental unit and sample size

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / animal models
quote: Results A review of the VPA literature showed that only 9% (3/34) of studies correctly determined that the experimental unit ( n ) was the litter and therefore made valid statistical inferences.
problem: Litter effects ignored; pups treated as independent n
need: Support litter (or cage) as a random/grouping factor and warn when pups from the same litter are counted as n

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / animal models
quote: In addition, litter effects accounted for up to 61% (p <0.001) of the variation in behavioural outcomes, which was larger than the treatment effects.
problem: Litter variance larger than treatment effect
need: Mixed model with litter random effect and variance-component output

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / animal models
quote: In addition, few studies reported using randomisation (12%) or blinding (18%), and none indicated that a sample size calculation or power analysis had been conducted.
problem: No randomisation, blinding or sample-size calculation
need: Built-in randomisation of animals to groups and a power calculator linked to the analysis

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / animal models
quote: Furthermore, they showed that the false positive rate increases with the number of offspring per litter; if the number of offspring per litter is 12 (total number of offspring = 72) then the false positive rate is 80%.
problem: False-positive rate explodes when offspring are counted as n
need: Show the effective n and the consequence of clustering before running a test

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology
workflow: cell physiology, multiple cells per animal
quote: Both groups therefore contain “ N * n ” cells, and such experiments are often incorrectly analyzed by performing statistical tests, such as t tests or ANOVA, taking the number of samples in each group as N * n .
problem: Cells from few animals analysed as N*n independent samples
need: Hierarchical data entry (animal > cell) with analysis on animal means or a nested/mixed model

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology
quote: Even when only two cells are used from each animal, the false-positive rate is >10%.
problem: Even small amounts of pseudoreplication double the false-positive rate
need: Warn as soon as more than one observation per experimental unit is analysed as independent

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology
quote: Here, hundreds of sparks are often recorded from each cell, and the degree of pseudoreplication produced by treating sparks as independent is enormous when it comes to addressing questions such as whether the amplitude or spatial spread of these sparks is altered.
problem: Event-level data (sparks) treated as independent
need: Accept multi-level event data (event > cell > animal) and summarise per unit before testing

role: peer-reviewed tutorial/critique, cellular physiology
workflow: cellular physiology, several cells per animal
quote: both equal to 0.3, the simulation found that P was <0.05 in 29% of trials. Since there were no real differences in this simulation, these 29% are all false positives.
problem: Comparing groups of animals using cells as n produces very high false-positive rates
need: Require an animal ID column for cell-level data and run nested (hierarchical) t-test/ANOVA or mixed model

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Treatments and measured responses can either be numerical or categorical. Different statistical tools are required to evaluate numerical and categorical treatments and responses ( Table 1 and Figure 2 ). Failing to make these distinctions may be the most common error in the analysis of data from experiments in cellular and molecular biology.
problem: Numerical vs categorical treatments/responses confused when choosing tests
need: Test chooser that starts from the data type of treatment and response and maps to the right test family

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: For example, many authors make the mistake of using a t test to compare proportions.
problem: t-tests run on proportions/percentages of cells
need: When the response is counts of cells with/without an event, route to contingency/logistic analysis and warn against t-tests on percentages

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Planning ahead allows one to avoid the common mistake of failing to randomize batches of data acquisition across experimental conditions.
problem: Batch/acquisition order confounded with treatment
need: Randomisation/plate-layout helper that spreads conditions across batches and records batch as a factor

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Treating technical replicates as biological replicates is called pseudoreplication and often produces low estimates of variance and erroneous test results.
problem: Technical replicates analysed as biological replicates
need: Separate columns/fields for technical vs biological replicates with automatic averaging of technical replicates

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Mistaking SEM for SD gives a false impression of low variability.
problem: SEM read as SD
need: Label error-bar type on the graph and default descriptive plots to SD

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Time-course studies are a common example of repeated measurements in molecular cell biology that require special handling of nonindependence with approaches such as mixed models.
problem: Time courses analysed as independent groups
need: Offer mixed-model repeated-measures analysis for time courses, tolerant of missing time points

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: I see figures with error bars that do not say what they describe, and error bars and P values for single, 'representative' experiments.
problem: Error bars without definition and statistics on a single representative experiment
need: Refuse to compute P values when only one independent experiment is entered; force legend text stating error-bar type and n

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Understanding the rudiments of statistics would stop experimental biologists from calculating a P value and a s.e.m. from triplicates from one representative experiment, and might stop the reviewers and editors from letting these pass unquestioned.
problem: P value and SEM computed from triplicate wells of one experiment
need: Distinguish technical triplicates from independent experiments in data entry and block inference on n=1

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: When N is only 2 or 3, it would be more transparent to just plot the independent data points, and let the readers interpret the data for themselves, rather than showing possibly misleading P values or error bars and drawing statistical inferences.
problem: Error bars and P values on N=2-3
need: For very small N, default to plotting individual independent points without inferential bars

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Statistics should not be shown for replicates because they merely indicate the fidelity with which the replicates were made, and have no bearing on the hypothesis being tested.
problem: Error bars/P values computed from replicate plates or wells
need: Treat replicate measurements as QC (show their spread separately) and use only independent experiments for inference

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Had we calculated and shown errors and P -values for replicates in Fig 3A , we might have incorrectly concluded, and perhaps misled the readers to conclude that there was a statistically significant effect of HH-CSF in stimulating Bjm transcription (see Fundamental principle 3 in Sidebar A ).
problem: qPCR/ELISA technical replicate wells used for significance testing
need: qPCR/ELISA templates that average technical wells per sample before any test

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Failure to take note of abnormal variation in replicates can lead to incorrect statistical inferences.
problem: Aberrant replicates not noticed
need: Flag replicate wells whose spread exceeds expected technical variation

role: peer-reviewed critique, experimental biology
quote: Abstract Error bars commonly appear in figures in publications, but experimental biologists are often unsure how they should be used and interpreted.
problem: Researchers unsure what error bars mean
need: Explain on-graph what each error-bar type shows and how to read overlap

role: peer-reviewed critique, experimental biology
quote: Because error bars can be descriptive or inferential, and could be any of the bars listed in Table I or even something else, they are meaningless, or misleading, if the figure legend does not state what kind they are.
problem: Figure legends do not state what error bars are
need: Auto-generate legend text with error-bar type and n

role: peer-reviewed critique, experimental biology
quote: If an experiment involves triplicate cultures, and is repeated four independent times, then n = 4, not 3 or 12.
problem: n miscounted from triplicate cultures
need: Compute n from the number of independent experiments entered, display it, and put it in the legend

role: peer-reviewed critique, experimental biology
quote: It is a common and serious error to conclude “no effect exists” just because P is greater than 0.05.
problem: P>0.05 interpreted as no effect
need: Report effect size with CI next to P and word non-significant results as inconclusive

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: Or try a different way to analyze the data: remove a few outliers; transform to logarithms; try a nonparametric test; redefine the outcome by normalizing (say, dividing by each animal’s weight); use a method to compare one variable while adjusting for differences in another; the list of possibilities is endless.
problem: Trying analyses until P<0.05 (P-hacking)
need: Keep an analysis log/audit trail of every test and transformation tried, exportable with the result

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: This is when you did not choose a sample size in advance, but just kept going until you liked the results.
problem: Ad hoc sample size: adding samples until significant
need: Record the planned n up front and flag analyses run on more data than planned

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: Pharmacology journals are full of graphs and tables showing the mean and the standard error of the mean (SEM). ... One problem with plotting or displaying the mean ± SEM is that some people viewing the graph or table may mistakenly think that the error bars show the variability of the data.
problem: Mean ± SEM is the default in pharmacology and is misread as data variability
need: Default to SD/raw points for variability and CI for precision; label SEM if chosen

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: Many scientists mistakenly believe that the chance of making a false positive conclusion is 5 %. In fact, in many situations, the chance of making a type I false positive conclusion is much higher than 5 %
problem: P < 0.05 is misread as a 5% chance the finding is false
need: Explain P values in plain language next to the result and show effect size with CI rather than only significance

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: My suggestion for authors: For each figure or table, clearly state whether or not the sample size was chosen in advance, and whether every step used to process and analyze the data was planned as part of the experimental protocol.
problem: Unclear whether sample size and processing steps were pre-planned
need: Methods export that states planned n and every processing step applied

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / life sciences
quote: Interpreting comparisons between two effects without directly comparing them The problem Researchers often base their conclusions regarding the impact of an intervention (such as a pre- vs. post-intervention difference or a correlation between two variables) by noting that the intervention yields a significant effect in the experimental condition or group, whereas the corresponding effect in the control condition or group is not significant.
problem: Concluding two effects differ because one is significant and the other is not
need: When users compare effects across groups, offer the interaction test (two-way ANOVA / compare slopes) directly

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / life sciences
workflow: repeated measures / multiple trials per subject
quote: Inflating the units of analysis The problem The experimental unit is the smallest observation that can be randomly and independently assigned, i.e. the number of independent values that are free to vary ( Parsons et al., 2018 ).
problem: Units of analysis inflated (trials or repeated measures counted as subjects)
need: Ask for the experimental unit and compute df from it

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / life sciences
quote: Spurious correlations most commonly arise if one or several outliers are present for one of the two variables.
problem: Correlations driven by single outliers
need: Always show the scatterplot with any correlation and offer robust correlation/outlier diagnostics

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / life sciences
quote: How to detect it Reviewers should pay particular attention to reported correlations that are not accompanied by a scatterplot and consider if sufficient justification has been provided when data points have been discarded.
problem: Correlations reported without scatterplots; discarded points unjustified
need: Pair every correlation result with its scatterplot and log any excluded points

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / life sciences
quote: Another problem related to small sample size is that the distribution of the sample is more likely to deviate from normality, and the limited sample size makes it often impossible to rigorously test the assumption of normality ( Ghasemi and Zahediasl, 2012 ).
problem: Normality untestable at small n
need: Warn when n is too small for normality tests and suggest showing data / nonparametric alternatives

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / life sciences
quote: Most commonly, circular analysis is used to divide (e.g. sub-grouping, binning) or reduce (e.g. defining a region of interest, removing ‘outliers’) the complete dataset using a selection criterion that is retrospective and inherently relevant to the statistical outcome.
problem: Circular analysis: selecting/excluding data with criteria tied to the outcome
need: Record exclusion/subgrouping criteria and when they were set; flag post-hoc exclusions in the audit trail

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / life sciences
quote: Failing to correct for multiple comparisons The problem When researchers explore task effects, they often explore the effect of multiple task conditions on multiple variables (behavioural outcomes, questionnaire items, etc.), sometimes with an underdetermined a priori hypothesis.
problem: No correction for multiple comparisons
need: Count tests performed in a project and offer family-wise/FDR correction by default

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience / life sciences
quote: How to detect it Flexibility of analysis is difficult to detect because researchers rarely disclose all the necessary information.
problem: Analytical flexibility undisclosed
need: Exportable analysis history listing every analysis run

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience (513 papers audited; abstract only, full text paywalled)
quote: We reviewed 513 behavioral, systems and cognitive neuroscience articles in five top-ranking journals ... and found that 78 used the correct procedure and 79 used the incorrect procedure.
problem: Difference between significant and non-significant treated as significant (no interaction test)
need: Steer 'does the effect differ between groups' questions to an interaction test and explain why

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience (513 papers audited; abstract only, full text paywalled)
quote: An additional analysis suggests that incorrect analyses of interactions are even more common in cellular and molecular neuroscience.
problem: Interaction errors most common at the bench (cellular/molecular)
need: Bench-facing tool must make the interaction test the default path for genotype x treatment designs

role: peer-reviewed critique, biostatistics (abstract only; full text paywalled)
quote: The reliability and reproducibility of science are under scrutiny. However, a major cause of this lack of repeatability is not being considered: the wide sample-to-sample variability in the P value.
problem: Over-reliance on single P values, which vary widely between replicate experiments
need: Report effect sizes with confidence intervals alongside P and explain P-value variability

role: peer-reviewed critique, biostatistics, Points of Significance (abstract only; full text paywalled)
quote: The meaning of error bars is often misinterpreted, as is the statistical significance of their overlap.
problem: Error-bar overlap misread as a significance test
need: Do not invite overlap-based inference: show the test result and CI of the difference explicitly

role: peer-reviewed critique, statistics news feature (standfirst only; full text paywalled)
quote: P values, the 'gold standard' of statistical validity, are not as reliable as many scientists assume.
problem: Overconfidence in P values
need: Present estimation (effect size + CI) as the primary result with P secondary

role: peer-reviewed editorial guidance, pharmacology
quote: For example, individual experimental (test) group values should not be normalized to the matched experimental control group values and subjected to parametric analysis since the experimental control group will have no variance
problem: Test values are divided by matched controls (control = 1, no variance) and then analysed parametrically
need: Detect a zero-variance control column after normalization and block parametric tests; offer ratio-paired or log-ratio one-sample analysis instead

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology (journal guidance editorial)
quote: If this is done, the correct units for such normalized data is % (or fold) of the control group's mean value, and graph Y axes and figure legends should be appropriately labelled to reflect this (‘fold’ or ‘% control’ is insufficiently clear).
problem: Ambiguous axis labels for normalised data
need: Auto-label normalised axes precisely ('fold of control mean' vs 'fold matched control')

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology (journal guidance editorial)
quote: Thus it is worth reiterating and emphasizing that, for example, when 6 samples are run 3 times each, the group size is 6, not 18, the SEM is the SD divided by √6, not √18, and the statistics should be done on 6 samples per group, not 18.
problem: Technical repeats counted in group size and SEM
need: Average technical repeats per sample automatically and compute SEM on samples

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology (journal guidance editorial)
quote: Some statistical packages may not permit analysis with group sizes below n = 5, whereas others may, thereby making it possible to obtain P < 0.05 with group sizes of less than 5.
problem: Software happily computes P on very small groups

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology (journal guidance editorial with compliance audit)

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology (journal guidance editorial with compliance audit)

problem: Non-Gaussian data analysed with parametric tests
need: Assumption check step with visible residual/QQ plots and suggestion of log transform or nonparametric test

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology (journal guidance editorial with compliance audit)

problem: Y axes of normalised data mislabelled

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology (journal guidance editorial with compliance audit)
quote: Outliers should therefore be included in data analysis and presentation unless a predefined and defensible set of exclusion criteria can be generated and applied.
problem: Outliers removed ad hoc
need: Outlier handling that requires a predefined rule, keeps excluded points visible and records the exclusion

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology (journal guidance editorial with compliance audit)
quote: In recently submitted studies that do not currently comply with our requirements, it is often the case that we find all of the following: a lack of randomization and blinding, unequal group sizes, and statistical analysis applied when n is <5.
problem: No randomisation/blinding, unequal n, statistics on n<5
need: Design helpers for randomisation and blinding plus small-n warnings

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology and pharmacology (audit of J Physiol / BJP papers)
quote: Overall, 76-84% of papers with written measures that summarized data variability used standard errors of the mean, and 90-96% of papers did not report exact p-values for primary analyses and post-hoc tests.
problem: SEM as variability measure and non-exact P values persist after editorial advice
need: Defaults: SD for variability, exact P everywhere

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology and pharmacology (audit of J Physiol / BJP papers)
quote: 76-84% of papers that plotted measures to summarize data variability used standard errors of the mean, and only 2-4% of papers plotted raw data used to calculate variability.
problem: Raw data almost never plotted
need: Plot raw data points by default with summary overlaid

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology and pharmacology (audit of J Physiol / BJP papers)
quote: Of papers that reported p-values between 0.05 and 0.1, 56-63% interpreted these as trends or statistically significant.
problem: P between 0.05 and 0.1 reported as 'trend' (spin)
need: Result wording generator that avoids 'trend' language and reports effect sizes with CIs

role: peer-reviewed critique, animal research (271 papers audited)
quote: Most of the papers surveyed did not use randomisation (87%) or blinding (86%), to reduce bias in animal selection and outcome assessment.
problem: Randomisation and blinding not used/reported
need: Built-in randomisation and blinding-code generator, recorded in the methods

role: peer-reviewed critique, animal research (271 papers audited)
quote: Only 70% of the publications that used statistical methods described their methods and presented the results with a measure of error or variability.
problem: Statistical methods or variability measures missing
need: Result export always includes method name and variability measure

role: peer-reviewed critique, animal research (271 papers audited)
quote: In 35% (69/198) of the papers that reported animal numbers in the methods section, the number of animals was either not reported in the results section, was unclear, or was different from that reported in the methods .
problem: Animal numbers inconsistent between methods and results
need: Carry n from the data into every result, legend and methods sentence automatically

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (271 animal studies), biomedical research
quote: We found that only 62% (75/121) of all the experiments assessed that were amenable to a factorial design (and analysis) reported using one
problem: Factorial designs/analyses are not used where the design calls for them
need: Recognise two crossed grouping variables in the data table and offer factorial (two-way) ANOVA with interaction

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (271 animal studies), biomedical research
quote: Only 8% of the 48 studies assessed presented raw data for individual animals
problem: Individual-animal data are almost never shown
need: Make individual data points visible in graphs and exportable as a data supplement by default

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical animal research, ARRIVE compliance
quote: Thirteen percent (95% confidence interval [CI] 8.7%–18.5%) of articles did not report statistical analyses at all, and only 39% (95% CI 32.5%–46.8%) correctly used non-parametric statistical tests on non-parametric neurological scoring data.
problem: Parametric tests on ordinal clinical scores
need: When data are ordinal scores, steer to nonparametric tests

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical animal research, ARRIVE compliance
quote: As many as 55% (95% CI 46.7%–62.3%) of studies, however, included analyses based on what we consider to be inappropriate statistical tests, and we saw no consistency in statistical tests of essentially the same hypothesis (part 2 in Text S1 ).
problem: Inappropriate and inconsistent tests for the same hypothesis
need: Consistent design-driven test recommendations

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical animal research, ARRIVE compliance
quote: Only 4% of EAE papers in these top-ranking journals (1/26; 95% CI 0.7%–18.9%) reported adequate use of a single non-parametric analysis of data on neurological scores, and 67% (95% CI 41.7%–84.8%) used only a t -test, which is not statistically justified [17] .
problem: Only t-tests used on score time courses
need: Score data templates with appropriate nonparametric/repeated-measures options

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical animal research, ARRIVE compliance
quote: We found that the percentage of studies, in the two years after endorsement of the ARRIVE guidelines, reporting blinding in their experimental design was similar to that in past surveys (20% in PLOS journals and 21% in Nature journals); however, fewer than 10% of the relevant studies in either Nature or PLOS journals reported randomisation (10% in PLOS journals and 0% in Nature journals), and even fewer mentioned any power/sample size analysis
problem: Randomisation and power analysis still unreported after ARRIVE
need: Power calculator and randomisation tool whose outputs flow into methods text

role: peer-reviewed critique, life sciences reporting (NPQIP collaborative)
quote: Reporting of the Landis 4 items The proportion of NPG in vivo studies reaching full compliance with the Landis 4 criteria increased from 0% (0/203) to 16.4% (31/189) (Χ²=36.1, df=1, p=1.8×10 −9 ), but remained significantly lower than the target of 80% (95% CI 11.6% to 22.6%, Wald test versus 80% z=−15.4, p=2.2×10 −16 ).
problem: Randomisation, blinding, sample size calculation and exclusions rarely all reported even with a checklist
need: Capture randomisation, blinding, sample-size rationale and exclusions in the project and emit them in the methods

role: peer-reviewed critique, life sciences reporting (NPQIP collaborative)
quote: There were more substantial improvements in the individual prevalences of reporting of randomisation, blinding, exclusions and sample size calculations for in vivo experiments, and less substantial improvements for in vitro experiments.
problem: In vitro studies almost never report randomisation/blinding/sample size/exclusions, even after a checklist
need: Bench (in vitro) workflows need the same design-reporting capture as animal work

role: peer-reviewed critique, in vivo research risk of bias
quote: Randomisation was reported in 662 publications (24.8%), blinded assessment of outcome in 788 (29.5%), a sample size calculation in 20 (0.7%), and a statement of potential conflict of interest in 308 (11.5%).
problem: Sample size calculation almost never reported
need: Integrated sample-size/power calculation stored with the project

role: peer-reviewed critique, in vivo research risk of bias
quote: Four of 146 (3%) reported the blinded assessment of outcome, 15 of 146 (10%) reported a conflict of interest statement, and none of the 146 reported a sample size calculation.
problem: Leading institutions' animal papers lack blinding and sample size calculations
need: Blinding and sample-size tools inside the analysis software

role: peer-reviewed critique with experiments, Western blot densitometry
quote: In the last decade, it has become apparent that assumptions underpinning these comparisons are often violated in studies reporting Western blot data in the literature. These violations can lead to erroneous interpretations of data and may contribute to poor reproducibility of research.
problem: Western blot densitometry is assumed proportional to protein amount without testing linearity or saturation
need: Fit a dilution series (proportional vs linear vs hyperbolic) and flag sample bands outside the linear range

role: peer-reviewed critique, Western blot densitometry
quote: We also confirm that when data to be normalised are not directly proportional to protein abundance, it is a mistake to use the normalisation technique of dividing densitometry data from the protein-of-interest with densitometry data from loading control protein(s), as this can cause the normalised data to be unusable for making comparisons.
problem: Dividing target by loading control when signals are non-proportional
need: Fit the signal-vs-load relationship (linear with intercept / hyperbolic) and normalise via the fitted curve, warning when ratio normalisation is invalid

role: peer-reviewed critique, Western blot densitometry
quote: It is commonly assumed that this model fits O.D. data [ 5 ], and only rarely are experimental data supporting this assumption included in published studies.
problem: Linearity of densitometry assumed without evidence
need: Ask for/accept a dilution series and report the linear range alongside results

role: peer-reviewed critique, Western blot densitometry
quote: It is inappropriate to quantitatively analyse saturated Western blot data as differences in protein/PTM abundance between samples can be missed, resulting in false-negative findings [ 3 , 4 , 8 , 12 , 13 ].
problem: Saturated bands quantified
need: Flag saturated/plateaued values when importing densitometry from image-analysis exports

role: peer-reviewed critique, Western blot quantification
quote: Since many labs typically load a specific, fixed amount of protein (typically between 10 and 50 μg) into the gel lanes without determining the optimal protein load, there is a strong potential for gel saturation, particularly for loading controls such as GAPDH, beta-actin, and tubulin.
problem: Fixed protein load saturates housekeeping loading controls
need: Linear-range helper: fit band density vs load and show where each protein saturates

role: peer-reviewed critique, Western blot quantification
quote: Furthermore, the housekeeping proteins themselves can be variably expressed between the experimental conditions, thereby eliminating their usefulness for the normalization of western blots [ 14 – 17 ].
problem: Housekeeping proteins vary with treatment
need: Support total-protein normalisation and test loading-control stability across conditions

role: peer-reviewed critique, Western blot experimental design
quote: Data Analysis: The Background Subtraction Problem Background subtraction is a common reason to obtain variable or incorrect data from western blots [ 27 ].
problem: Background subtraction errors
need: Record the background-subtraction method with imported densitometry values

role: peer-reviewed methods critique, Western blot quantification
quote: There are numerous calculations from densitometric data using formulas buried in EXCEL spreadsheets spanning multiple worksheets and files to obtain quantitative data from western blots. It is often difficult to follow the basis of the calculations and we have found that when lab members are faced with the direct question of how to work up the raw data obtained from western blots to publishable results, there is often confusion.
problem: Densitometry is worked up in opaque multi-sheet Excel formulas and lab members are unsure how to do it
need: Provide a transparent, documented Western blot workflow (background-subtracted density -> loading-control normalisation -> fold change -> stats) from imported densitometry tables

role: peer-reviewed critique, Western blot experimental design
quote: To alleviate the effect of membrane saturation, a standard curve of protein load versus band density should be produced for each target protein.
problem: No standard curve of load vs density
need: Built-in standard-curve fit for each target with linear-range reporting

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR (MIQE 2.0 editorial)
quote: Nevertheless, an examination of the methods section generally reveals serious problems with the experimental workflow, ranging from poorly documented sample handling to absent assay validation, inappropriate normalisation, missing PCR efficiency calculations and nonexistent statistical justification.
problem: qPCR papers lack efficiency calculations, valid normalisation and statistics
need: qPCR module that requires efficiencies (or standard curves), supports multiple reference genes and outputs a MIQE-style methods summary

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR (MIQE 2.0 editorial)
quote: Assay efficiencies are assumed, not measured [ 18 , 19 , 20 ].
problem: PCR efficiency assumed to be 100%
need: Efficiency-corrected (Pfaffl-type) calculation from standard curves by default, with a warning when 2^-ddCq is used without efficiency data

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR (MIQE 2.0 editorial)
quote: Fold-changes of 1.2- or 1.5-fold are routinely reported as biologically meaningful, even at low expression levels, without any assessment of measurement uncertainty or technical variance [ 14 , 15 ].
problem: Small fold changes reported without uncertainty
need: Report fold changes with confidence intervals propagated from Cq variability

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR (MIQE 2.0 editorial)
quote: Normalisation is based on reference genes that are neither stable nor validated [ 21 , 22 , 23 ].
problem: Unvalidated reference genes
need: Reference-gene stability check (geNorm/NormFinder-style) and multi-reference normalisation

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR and biomedical reproducibility
quote: Every single publication uses a single, unvalidated reference gene for normalisation (all old favourites), all use the 2 −ΔΔCq method with no attempt to calculate PCR efficiency and reporting of RNA quality control measures is non-existent.
problem: Single unvalidated reference gene and 2^-ddCq without efficiency
need: qPCR analysis that defaults to multiple reference genes and efficiency correction, flagging single-reference designs

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR and biomedical reproducibility
quote: Unfortunately, researchers themselves are far less enthusiastic and in addition to the thousands of peer-reviewed papers that are already published, thousands more are published every year without regard for the MIQE guidelines and report results and conclusions that are unlikely to be correct [57] , [58] .
problem: MIQE guidelines ignored
need: Embed MIQE-relevant checks in the analysis rather than as a separate checklist

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR in colorectal cancer research (179 papers audited)
quote: Using even these minimal evaluation criteria, the validity of only three percent (6/179) of the publications can be adequately assessed.
problem: qPCR results unassessable for validity
need: Export qPCR results with the reference-gene validation, efficiencies and method used

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR in colorectal cancer research (179 papers audited)
quote: In 92% of the publications, only a single reference gene was used.
problem: Single reference gene normalisation
need: Support and encourage geometric mean of multiple reference genes

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR in colorectal cancer research (179 papers audited)
quote: Validation of the reference genes and online supplemental data were not reported in 87%–92% of the publications.
problem: Reference gene validation not reported
need: Stability analysis of candidate reference genes included in the qPCR workflow and report

role: peer-reviewed critique, qPCR in colorectal cancer research (179 papers audited)

problem: ddCq assumptions (equal, stable efficiencies) not checked
need: Check target vs reference efficiency agreement before allowing 2^-ddCq

venue: American Journal of Physiology - Lung Cellular and Molecular Physiology

need: Flow-data import that keeps MFI and %-of-parent as distinct typed variables with appropriate tests for each

venue: American Journal of Physiology - Lung Cellular and Molecular Physiology
role: peer-reviewed critique, flow cytometry reporting

need: Methods text that names the summary statistic (median MFI, % of parent) used

venue: American Journal of Physiology - Lung Cellular and Molecular Physiology

need: Record compensation and gating provenance with imported flow statistics

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical infection/survival studies

need: Survival analysis that reports median survival difference with CI and flags tiny absolute differences that are 'significant'

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical infection/survival studies
quote: In the nonparametric analysis of survival data, the order of the events rather than the timing of the events is the basis for assessing differences between treatment groups.
problem: Log-rank significance confused with biological size of survival benefit
need: Show median survival and restricted-mean survival differences alongside the log-rank P

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical infection/survival studies

problem: Cage effects confounded with treatment in survival studies

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical oncology mouse models (400 papers audited)

problem: Mouse oncology papers omit most ARRIVE items
need: Project metadata capture (strain, sex, age, endpoints) that flows into the methods

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical oncology mouse models (400 papers audited)
quote: Most studies reported monitoring experimental animals for days to weeks post-tumour induction and before euthanasia, and 52% reported some sort of “survival analysis” using methods for time to event data (e.g. Kaplan-Meier estimates, Cox proportional hazards regression). need: Survival data entry that records the event definition (humane endpoint criteria) and censoring reason

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical oncology mouse models (400 papers audited)

need: Animal metadata fields in the data table

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical oncology (xenograft tumour growth statistics)

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical oncology (xenograft tumour growth statistics)

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical oncology (xenograft tumour growth statistics)
quote: However, the classic implementation of this analysis found in common laboratory software packages is severely limited by the requirement of equally spaced and complete data for each mouse over the entire study period, as well as the assumptions of equal variance at all time points and equal correlation between repeated measurements regardless of the length of time (lag) between the two observations.

role: peer-reviewed methods critique, in vitro dose-response (IC50)

role: peer-reviewed methods critique, in vitro dose-response (IC50)

problem: Different software/starting values give different IC50s or no fit

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical research statistical reporting (scoping review)
quote: Results revealed that a large proportion of articles insufficiently describe tests (median 44.8%, IQR [33.3–62.5%], k = 16 journals), software (31%, IQR [22.3–39.6%]) or sample sizes (44.2%, IQR [35.7–55.4%]).
problem: Tests, software and sample sizes insufficiently described
need: Auto-generated methods paragraph naming test, software version and exact n per group

quote: A notable proportion of articles (median 18.3%, IQR [6.79–26.7%]), k = 16) present contradictory information. problem: Methods and figure legends contradict each other on tests or sample sizes
need: Generate legends and methods from the same analysis record so tests and n cannot disagree

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical research statistical reporting (scoping review)
quote: The most frequently used tests were one way analysis of variance (ANOVA; used in 53.15% of articles, k = 223 articles), two way ANOVA (28.83%), repeated measure one way ANOVA (9.46%), unpaired Student’s t test (38.74%) and Student’s t test of undefined laterality (26.83% of articles).
problem: t-tests reported without stating one- or two-tailed
need: Results always state tails and paired/unpaired

role: peer-reviewed critique, preclinical research statistical reporting (scoping review)

need: GUI tool must emit complete, reproducible reporting text and analysis records by default

role: peer-reviewed critique, image-based figures in cell biology, physiology, plant science (580 papers)

problem: Image figures lack scale bars, inset markings, colour explanations
need: Figure-layout tool with scale bar, inset and label checks

role: peer-reviewed critique, image-based figures in cell biology, physiology, plant science (580 papers)
quote: Papers without any colorblind accessible figures were uncommon (3% to 6%); however, 45% of cell biology papers and 21% to 24% of physiology and plant science papers contained some images that were inaccessible to readers with deuteranopia ( Fig 2A ).

need: Colour-blind-safe channel colour presets (magenta/green) and a CVD preview

role: peer-reviewed critique, image-based figures in cell biology, physiology, plant science (580 papers)
quote: Our analysis revealed that 10% to 29% of papers screened failed to provide any scale information and that another third only provided incomplete scale information ( Fig 1B ).
problem: Missing scale bars on images
need: Layout tool that requires/automatically inserts scale information

role: peer-reviewed critique, science communication / colour maps
quote: At one point, most of the common software programmes applied rainbow as their default palette (e.g., MatLab, Paraview, VisAd, IrisExplorer) despite issues surrounding colour maps like rainbow, and variations thereof, being known for some time 9 – 20 .
problem: Software defaults to rainbow/jet colour maps
need: Ship perceptually uniform, CVD-safe default colour maps

role: peer-reviewed critique, science communication / colour maps
quote: For most scientists, the choice of colour maps has become almost passive, with the unscientific rainbow-like colour palette being commonplace.
problem: Colour map choice left to defaults
need: Good defaults matter more than options: make the safe palette the default

role: peer-reviewed critique, science communication / colour maps
quote: Building a colour map on a purely physical rather than a perceptual basis significantly alters how we perceive data; it adds artificial boundaries to some parts of the data range, hiding small-scale variations elsewhere, it prevents any visual intuitive order occurring in the data set, and renders the data unreadable for readers with common colour-vision deficiencies (Fig. 2 ).
problem: Non-perceptual colour maps distort data and exclude CVD readers
need: Perceptually uniform sequential/diverging maps for heat maps

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: Results: The agonist responses have unequal standard errors, as often seen in data like these concentration-response curves with responses expressed as change from baseline.
problem: Unequal variance across doses ignored in concentration-response analysis
need: Show residual-vs-fitted spread and suggest log transform or weighting

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: Expressing the data as absolute blood pressure and then transforming it to log blood pressure eliminated the heteroscedasticity, but made evident an effect of the inhibitor on baseline blood pressure.

need: Offer analysis on absolute and log-transformed scales and show baseline differences

need: Offer 'experiment' as a blocking factor in data entry and analysis

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
workflow: cell culture experiments run in blocks
quote: The data were ‘normalized' to be a percentage of the control value from each experiment, and thus the relative variability in the different treatments is distorted and the actual values are obscured.
problem: Normalised graphs hide raw values and distort variability
need: Plot raw paired values (before-after lines per experiment) as an alternative to % control bars

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: A scenario, in which an experimenter performed an experiment in two separate stages, combined the control groups for analysis and found some surprising results, is presented.
problem: Controls from separate experiments pooled
need: Keep experiment/stage as a factor and warn when non-contemporaneous controls are combined

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: The failure of pharmacological researchers to universally adopt the box and whisker plot may be the result of several interrelated obstacles.
problem: Box plots underused
need: Make box-and-whisker plots (with points) a one-click default for n>=5

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology and pharmacology (joint statistics series)
quote: They look around for an easy way to deal with their data, and often ask someone with possibly more experience but probably no more training what to do.
problem: Analysis choices copied from colleagues without training
need: In-tool guidance explaining choices, rather than relying on lab lore

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology and pharmacology (joint statistics series)
quote: The advice is often ‘well, this is what I did …’, almost designed to sustain the status quo and perhaps perpetuate error.
problem: Errors perpetuated by habit
need: Defaults that encode good practice so habit leads to correct output

role: peer-reviewed critique, medical research statistics (review of 47 common errors)
quote: Unfortunately, even simple and basic procedures such as the popular t-tests or chi-square tests are frequently misused in medical research, because their test assumptions are not evaluated sufficiently before application
problem: t-tests and chi-square applied without checking assumptions
need: Assumption checks (normality, variance, expected counts) surfaced before results

role: peer-reviewed critique, medical research statistics (review of 47 common errors)
quote: The standard error of the mean (SEM), although commonly and erroneously used for statistical description (perhaps because it makes data seem less variable), is not a descriptive statistic, but rather an inferential method used for statistical estimation
problem: SEM used as descriptive statistic
need: Descriptive tables default to SD; SEM only offered for inference with explanation

role: peer-reviewed critique, medical research statistics (review of 47 common errors)

problem: mean ± SD notation confusable with CI
need: Export descriptive results as mean (SD) with the statistic named

role: peer-reviewed critique, medical research statistics (review of 47 common errors)
quote: If a study contains multiple endpoints necessitating multiple statistical tests, it is important to check the rate of false positive results and the potential inflation of type I errors by applying adequate multiple-comparison corrections
problem: Multiple endpoints tested without correction
need: Project-level multiplicity tracker with correction options

role: peer-reviewed critique, medical research statistics (review of 47 common errors)
quote: Failure to specify/define all tests used clear and correctly Failure to state number of tails Failure to state if test was paired or unpaired Wrong names for statistical tests

role: peer-reviewed critique, biomedical statistical reporting guideline

venue: SAMPL Guidelines (EQUATOR Network / Science Editors' Handbook)
role: statistical reporting guideline, biomedical journals

problem: Errors concentrate in basic statistics (t-tests, chi-square, descriptive stats) rather than advanced methods
need: Put guardrails on the basic tests most researchers use: design questions, assumption checks and complete reporting

role: peer-reviewed critique, biomedical statistical reporting guideline
quote: Report the upper and lower boundaries of interpercentile ranges and the minimum and maximum values of ranges, not just the size of the range • Do NOT use the standard error of the mean (SE) to indicate the variability of a data set.

need: Descriptive output with SD/IQR boundaries; SE not offered as variability

role: peer-reviewed critique, experimental biology data analysis (estimation statistics)
quote: However, a major obstacle to adopting estimation plots is accessibility to suitable software.
problem: No accessible software for estimation (effect size + CI) plots
need: Built-in estimation plots (Gardner-Altman / Cumming) for two-group and multi-group comparisons

role: methods preprint, experimental biology data analysis
quote: The analyst then plots the two groups’ means in a bar chart and denotes ‘significance’ by marking it with a star ... First, by displaying only the means and width of their errors, a bar chart obscures the observed values
problem: Bar chart plus significance star hides both the data and the effect size
need: Offer estimation plots (all points plus mean difference with bootstrap 95% CI) as an alternative to stars

role: peer-reviewed critique, experimental biology data analysis (estimation statistics)
quote: As these estimation methods require only minimal statistical retraining, they have great potential to shift the current data-analysis culture away from dichotomous thinking towards quantitative reasoning
problem: Dichotomous significant/not-significant thinking
need: Results pages lead with effect size and CI

role: peer-reviewed critique, biostatistics education for basic scientists
quote: This includes using incorrect or suboptimal tests [ 1 , 2 ], summarizing data that were analyzed by nonparametric techniques as mean and standard deviation or standard error [ 4 ], reporting p -values that are inconsistent with the test statistic [ 5 , 6 ], p-hacking [ 7 ], and analyzing nonindependent data as though they are independent [ 3 ].
problem: Nonparametric results summarised as mean ± SD/SE; P inconsistent with test statistic
need: Match summary statistics to the test (median/IQR with nonparametric tests) and compute P from the reported statistic

role: peer-reviewed critique, biostatistics education for basic scientists
quote: According to our recent systematic review [ 4 ], 97.2% of original research papers published in the top 25% of physiology journals ( n = 683/703) included some form of statistical analysis ( Fig 1A ).
problem: Nearly every paper needs statistics but training is optional

role: peer-reviewed critique, biostatistics education for basic scientists
quote: Biostatistics was not required or offered as an elective course for students in 12.5% of departments.
problem: Some PhD programmes offer no biostatistics at all
need: Embedded learning material in the analysis tool

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology journal statistics policy editorial
quote: However, there was a general consensus that the ‘duplication’ of work required to complete and check this document was an unnecessary and excessive time burden.
problem: Manually compiling a statistical summary document duplicates work
need: Generate the statistical summary (test, n, mean, SD, exact P) automatically from the analysis

role: peer-reviewed critique, physiology journal statistics policy editorial
quote: These requirements include, but are not limited to: (1) providing a statistical summary document for revised research articles, which is included as Supporting Information in the published paper; (2) using SD, not SEM (unless clearly justified and exempted); (3) providing mean and SD values in the text and statistical summary document; (4) providing precise P‐ values; and (5) providing all underlying data
problem: Journals require SD not SEM, exact P and underlying data
need: Export bundle with SD, exact P values and the raw data table

role: peer-reviewed critique, ligand-binding assay calibration (abstract; full text scanned PDF)
