problem: ELISA/ligand-binding standard curves fitted with linear models
need: Standard-curve interpolation defaulting to 4PL/5PL with the usable range reported

role: peer-reviewed critique, ligand-binding assay calibration (abstract; full text scanned PDF)
quote: Alternative models should be used with caution and with knowledge of the accuracy and precision performance of the model across the entire calibration range, but particularly at upper and lower analyte concentration areas, where the 4-and 5-PL algorithms generally outperform alternative models.
problem: Inaccurate interpolation at the ends of the standard curve
need: Flag samples interpolated near or beyond the curve asymptotes / outside the calibrator range

role: peer-reviewed critique, ligand-binding assay calibration (abstract; full text scanned PDF)
quote: The fit of the experimental data to the model should be evaluated by assessment of agreement of nominal and model-predicted data for calibrators.
problem: Calibration fit not checked by back-calculating calibrators
need: Show back-calculated calibrator recovery (%) for every standard-curve fit

role: peer-reviewed critique, ligand-binding assay calibration (abstract; full text scanned PDF)
quote: Incorporation of weighting into the model requires additional effort but generally results in improved calibration curve performance.
problem: Unweighted fits despite heteroscedastic assay response
need: One-click weighting options (1/Y^2 etc.) for standard curves

role: peer-reviewed critique, flow cytometry reporting standard
quote: Furthermore, the lack of reporting standardization limits collaboration, independent validation/refutation and meta-analysis, and thus minimizes the value of the wealth of existing flow cytometry data due to poor annotation ( 2 ).
problem: Flow cytometry data poorly annotated, unreproducible
need: Keep gating/compensation metadata attached to the population statistics used in the analysis

role: peer-reviewed critique, flow cytometry reporting standard
quote: The overall gating strategy shall be traceable up to the set of all events.
problem: Gating hierarchy not traceable in reported statistics
need: Import population statistics with their full gate path (e.g. Live/Singlets/CD4+)

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: Our data show that most bar and line graphs present mean ± SE. ... Showing the SE rather than the SD magnifies the apparent visual differences between groups.
problem: Mean ± SEM is the default error bar, making group differences look larger than the data support
need: Make SD (or individual points) the default for describing data, label SEM explicitly, and explain the difference at the point of choice

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: Bar graphs of paired data erroneously suggest that the groups being compared are independent and provide no information about whether changes are consistent across individuals
problem: Paired/before-after data are plotted as independent bars, hiding within-subject changes
need: When the design is paired, offer before-after (connected points) plots and a plot of the paired differences by default

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: 213 papers (95% of the papers that used ANOVA) did not contain all information needed to determine what type of ANOVA was performed, including the names and number of factors and whether each factor was entered as a between-subjects or within-subjects factor.
problem: Papers do not state which ANOVA (factors, between vs within) was run
need: Auto-generate a methods sentence naming each factor, its levels, and whether it is between- or within-subjects, plus the post-hoc test

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: 72.8% of papers (164/225) stated what test was used to examine pairwise differences after performing an ANOVA (such as Tukey and Bonferroni). The remaining 27.1% of papers (61/225) did not specify what type of post-hoc tests were performed.
problem: Post-hoc test after ANOVA is not named
need: Record and print the post-hoc/multiple-comparison method and the comparison family in the results and methods text

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: Most of the papers (95.7%; 156/163) did not report the t-statistic (column 2) and over two-thirds (69.3%; 113/163) did not report exact p-values
problem: Test statistics, degrees of freedom and exact P values are omitted, so results cannot be checked
need: Report t/F, df and exact P by default in result tables and copy-ready text

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (systematic review), physiology
quote: A more recent study of papers reporting the results of experiments that examined the effects of prenatal interventions on offspring found that the statistical analyses in 46% of the papers were invalid because authors failed to account for non-independent observations
problem: Offspring from the same litter are analysed as independent observations
need: Capture litter/dam as a grouping column and analyse at the litter level or with a mixed model

role: peer-reviewed methods perspective, data visualization
quote: This is problematic, as standard line graphs do not show values for individual participants. The sample size for each group cannot be determined, nor can the viewer assess whether response patterns are similar for all individuals in a particular group.
problem: Line graphs of means hide individual trajectories and per-group n
need: Offer line graphs with individual traces (spaghetti) or shaded spread plus per-time-point n

role: peer-reviewed methods perspective, data visualization
quote: making it difficult to determine where the error bars for each group end. Several strategies are used to address this problem. The most common approach is to use error bars to show the standard error
problem: Overlapping error bars in multi-group line graphs are 'solved' by switching to the smaller SEM
need: Render spread as semi-transparent bands or offset points instead of shrinking error bars to SEM

role: peer-reviewed methods paper, data visualization
quote: Although bar graphs are designed for categorical data, they are routinely used to present continuous data in studies that have small sample sizes. ... To address this problem, many journals have implemented new policies that require authors to show the data distribution.
problem: Journals now require showing data distributions, but bar graphs remain the routine output for small-sample continuous data
need: Provide no-code univariate scatter, box and violin plots with overlaid points as first-class graph types

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (survey of PhD programs), physiology
quote: show that the ability to understand statistical concepts and apply statistical skills is essential for research; however, biostatistics training is not always required to complete a PhD.
problem: Many bench scientists receive no required statistics training
need: Embed plain-language explanations of why a test or graph was chosen and what its assumptions are, inside the analysis workflow

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (survey of PhD programs), physiology
quote: The authors could not determine whether animals were excluded or did not complete the experiment in 64.2% of stroke studies and 72.9% of cancer studies.
problem: Exclusions/attrition of animals are not reported, so n analysed differs silently from n enrolled
need: Track excluded data points with a reason and report n enrolled vs n analysed per group automatically

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (survey of PhD programs), physiology
workflow: in vitro replicates, neurons per animal, litters
quote: Many basic biomedical scientists do not recognize that these designs include nonindependent data ... This leads to confusion in the published literature. Some authors do not specify how clustered data were analyzed, whereas others analyze the data as though all points were independent.
problem: Clustered designs (replicates within experiments, neurons within animals, pups within litters) are analysed as independent
need: Ask for the clustering variable during data entry and aggregate or use a nested model before testing

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (survey of PhD programs), physiology
quote: Statistics programs vary among institutions; therefore, young investigators often need to choose between purchasing an expensive individual license or learning to use a new statistics program each time that they move.
problem: Institution-bound commercial licences force early-career scientists to buy software or relearn a new program after each move
need: Be free/portable so analyses and skills move with the researcher

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (survey of PhD programs), physiology
quote: Programs that have a user interface often make decisions about what test to use based on the characteristics of the data. Investigators who use these programs may have less knowledge of the specific tests that are being performed or how they are implemented in the statistical software package.
problem: Point-and-click programs choose tests implicitly so users do not know what was run
need: Make the chosen test, its assumptions and the reason for the choice explicit and editable rather than silent

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (automated screen of 227,998 papers), 23 biomedical fields
quote: In two of these fields, complementary and alternative medicine and pharmacology and pharmaceutical sciences, more informative graphs are not commonly used. Interventions in these fields may need to provide more information about how to determine what type of more informative graphs is best for one’s dataset, and how to make more informative graphs.
problem: Researchers do not know which informative graph suits their dataset or how to make it
need: Recommend a graph type from n, design (paired/clustered) and variable type, with one-click creation

role: peer-reviewed viewpoint, cell biology
quote: when each cell measurement is treated as an independent sample, the standard error of the mean is always tiny, whether or not there is variability among experimental replicates.
problem: Hundreds of cells are used as n, giving tiny SEMs and P values that ignore run-to-run variability
need: Require a replicate/experiment column; compute SEM and P from per-replicate means while plotting all cells (SuperPlot)

role: peer-reviewed viewpoint, cell biology

need: One-click SuperPlot from long-format data: colour by replicate, auto-compute replicate means, run the test on those means

role: peer-reviewed viewpoint, cell biology
quote: By encoding the biological replicate into the data, such trends can be revealed without normalizing to a control group: P values can then be calculated using statistical tests that take into account linkages among samples (e.g., a paired or ratio
problem: Run-to-run differences in absolute values are removed by normalizing to control instead of pairing by experiment
need: Allow pairing/blocking by experiment (paired or ratio t-test, RM ANOVA) and linked points per run as an alternative to normalization

role: peer-reviewed viewpoint, cell biology
workflow: figure legends for cell biology data
quote: Whatever way authors choose to display their data, it is critical to list the number of independent experiments in the figure or caption, as well as how the means and statistical tests were calculated.
problem: Figure captions omit the number of independent experiments and how statistics were computed
need: Auto-write the legend with number of independent experiments, cells per experiment, and the level at which the test was done

role: peer-reviewed critique with audit, neuroscience
quote: 37% of the time (and not 5%) the null hypotheses would be (erroneously) rejected. Thus when there is a positive correlation, null hypotheses will be rejected too often
problem: Correlated (non-independent) observations inflate the false-positive rate far above 5%
need: Warn when multiple rows share a subject/animal ID and the chosen test assumes independence; offer averaging or a mixed model

role: peer-reviewed critique with audit, neuroscience
quote: For example, 96-well plates often contain small amounts of fluid, and wells near the edges of the plate may evaporate faster than wells in the centre, and thus alter the concentration of substances such as metabolites, secreted hormones, etc. Placing the control samples in the first column of the plate and the treated samples in the second column would therefore not be a good idea.

need: Generate randomised plate layouts and keep well position as a variable that can be checked for edge effects

role: peer-reviewed meta-research, animal and cell-culture experiments

role: peer-reviewed meta-research, animal and cell-culture experiments

need: Distinguish experimental, biological and observational units at data entry and reduce data to one value per experimental unit before testing

role: peer-reviewed meta-research, animal and cell-culture experiments
quote: a simple solution to the problem of pseudoreplication is to reduce the data to a single value for each EU. problem: Researchers lack an easy way to summarise subsamples (mean, slope, AUC) per experimental unit before analysis
need: Provide a 'summarise per experimental unit' step (mean, median, slope, AUC) that feeds the statistical test

role: peer-reviewed tutorial/critique, cellular physiology
quote: A better approach is to use hierarchical (nested) analysis or linear mixed modeling, which takes explicit account of the structure of the data, specifically how many cells come from each animal.
problem: Simple averaging per animal ignores unequal cells per animal; nested models are not used
need: Offer nested t-test / nested one-way ANOVA / mixed models that handle unequal numbers of cells per animal

role: peer-reviewed tutorial/critique, cellular physiology
quote: This identification of cells is not normally performed in the literature and is worth considering to give a graphical impression of the degree of clustering.
problem: Plots do not identify which cells came from which animal
need: Colour/shape points by animal in dot plots by default when an animal ID exists

role: peer-reviewed guidance/critique, cell and molecular biology
workflow: cell counts in categories (e.g. mitotic index)
quote: Proportions (e.g., 0.84 interphase cells and 0.16 mitotic cells) and percentages (e.g., 84% interphase cells and 16% mitotic cells) are also categorical responses but are often inappropriately treated as numerical responses in statistical test ... They may think that proportions are numerical responses, because they are numbers, but they are not numerical responses.
problem: Percentages/proportions of counted cells are analysed with t-tests
need: Accept the underlying counts and offer chi-square/Fisher or binomial/logistic models; warn when a t-test is run on proportions

role: peer-reviewed guidance/critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: For example, in an experiment with three treatments and a control the total type I error across the tests rises up to 0.3 with six pairwise
problem: Multiple pairwise t-tests are run instead of one ANOVA with post-hoc correction
need: When more than two groups are present, steer to ANOVA plus a corrected post-hoc test and show the family-wise error

role: peer-reviewed guidance/critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Unfortunately, authors commonly use SEM for error bars without appreciating that it is not a measure of true variation and, at best, is difficult to interpret as a description of the significance of the differences of group mean
problem: SEM error bars are used as if they described variation or significance
need: Prefer SD or 95% CI error bars by default and state which is shown

role: peer-reviewed guidance/critique, cell and molecular biology
workflow: imaging / assays run over several days

problem: Conditions are processed in separate batches/days, confounding treatment with batch
need: Provide randomised/blocked run schedules and record batch/day so it can be included as a blocking factor

role: peer-reviewed guidance/critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: Unfortunately, researchers often fail to provide sufficient detail (e.g., software options, test assumptions) for others to repeat the analysis. Many papers report p values that appear improbable based on simple inspection of the data and without specifying the statistical test used.
problem: Software options, assumptions and even the test used are not reported
need: Export an analysis record (software version, options, assumptions checked, test) alongside results

role: peer-reviewed comment by journal reviewer, cell and molecular biology
quote: The incidence of papers in cell and molecular biology that have basic statistical mistakes is alarming. I see figures with error bars that do not say what they describe
problem: Error bars in figures are not described
need: Never export a graph with error bars without an auto-generated legend stating what they represent and n

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: We have made just one comparison, so n = 1, no matter how many replicate plates we count.
problem: Replicate plates from one cell suspension (one mouse) are used to compute P values
need: Distinguish replicates from independent repeats and only allow inferential statistics across independent repeats

role: peer-reviewed critique, cell and molecular biology
quote: To remedy this, we could simply start the y -axis at 40 rather than zero ( Fig 1D ), to emphasize the differences in the response to HH-CSF. ... Also, axes should commence at 0, other than in exceptional circumstances, such as for log scales.
problem: Bar-graph y-axes are truncated to exaggerate differences
need: Start bar/column axes at zero by default and warn when a bar axis is truncated

role: peer-reviewed critique, experimental biology
quote: the value of n (i.e., the sample size, or the number of independently performed experiments) must be stated in the figure legend.
problem: The number of independent experiments (n) is missing from figure legends
need: Propagate n per group into the legend text and flag groups with unequal n

role: peer-reviewed critique, experimental biology
quote: Error bars can only be used to compare the experimental to control groups at any one time point. problem: Readers judge within-group (repeated) changes from between-group error bars
need: For repeated measures, plot the paired differences with their CI and analyse with paired/RM tests

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: P-Hacking. This is when you reanalyze a data set in many different ways, or perhaps reanalyze with additional replicates, until you get the result you want. ... From my conversations with scientists, it seems that this rule is commonly broken in reports of basic research.
problem: Data are reanalysed in many ways or replicates are added until P < 0.05
need: Keep an analysis log of every test run on a dataset and flag when n was increased after looking at P; support a pre-specified analysis plan

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: The other meaning of “significant” is that an effect is large enough to have a substantial physiological or clinical impact. These two meanings are completely different, but are often confused.
problem: Statistical significance is confused with biological importance
need: Report the effect size and its CI prominently and avoid the bare word 'significant' in generated text

role: peer-reviewed critique, pharmacology
quote: I suspect that one of the reasons that the results reported in many papers cannot be reproduced is that statistical analyses are often done as a quick afterthought, with the goal to sprinkle asterisks on figures and the word “significant” on conclusions.
problem: Statistics are bolted on at the end to decorate figures with asterisks
need: Plan the analysis with the design, and show effect sizes/CIs alongside any significance annotations

venue: Nature Neuroscience (author institutional repository record, UvA-DARE)
role: peer-reviewed meta-research (513 articles), neuroscience
workflow: comparing effects across groups (e.g. drug effect in WT vs KO)
quote: In practice, this comparison is often based on an incorrect procedure involving two separate tests in which researchers conclude that effects differ when one effect is significant (P < 0.05) but the other is not (P > 0.05). An additional analysis suggests that incorrect analyses of interactions are even more common in cellular and molecular neuroscience.
problem: Two effects are declared different because one is significant and the other is not, without testing the interaction
need: When the question is whether an effect differs between groups (e.g. genotype x treatment), run and report the interaction term of a two-way ANOVA

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience and life sciences
workflow: correlations and group inference with repeated observations
quote: For example, when inferring group results, the experimental unit is the number of subjects tested, rather than the number of observations made within each subject. But unfortunately, researchers tend to mix up these measures, resulting in both conceptual and practical issues.
problem: Observations within subjects are pooled as if they were independent subjects (e.g. pre and post pooled into one correlation)
need: Ask for subject ID and prevent pooling repeated observations into one correlation/test; offer per-timepoint or mixed analyses

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience and life sciences
workflow: many outcomes or many cells/time points
quote: In such cases, researchers are technically deploying statistical tests within every voxel/cell/timepoint, thereby increasing the likelihood of detecting a false positive result, due to the large number of measures included in the design.
problem: Many outcomes/cells/timepoints are tested without correction
need: Count the tests run on a dataset and apply/offer FDR or family-wise correction by default

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience and life sciences
quote: misinterpreting the results of a statistical test when the outcome is ... significant is also highly problematic but extremely common. ... This error is very common and should be highlighted as problematic.
problem: Non-significant results are interpreted as evidence of no effect
need: Report effect size with CI for non-significant results and avoid 'no difference' wording; offer equivalence testing

role: peer-reviewed critique, neuroscience and life sciences
quote: When a sample size is small, one can only detect large effects, thereby leaving high uncertainty around the estimate of the true effect size and leading to an overestimation of the actual effect size
problem: Small samples produce inflated effect sizes and unsupported claims
need: Provide a priori power / sensitivity analysis showing the smallest detectable effect for the chosen n

role: peer-reviewed editorial guidance, pharmacology
quote: However, unfortunately, in preclinical research, experiments are often not blinded.
problem: Preclinical experiments are not blinded
need: Support blinded group codes during data entry/analysis and unblind only at the end, recording that blinding was used

role: peer-reviewed editorial with compliance audit, pharmacology
quote: Table 1 illustrates that the outcome has not been as successful as we had hoped. Table 1. Many papers published in BJP do not adhere to all the journal's guidance
problem: Even papers declaring compliance with journal statistical guidance fail on equal n, randomisation, blinding, Y-axis labels for normalized data and correct post hoc tests
need: Build the journal checklist into the analysis: flag unequal n, missing randomisation/blinding statements, wrong axis label on normalized data, and parametric post hoc on zero-variance controls

role: peer-reviewed editorial with compliance audit, pharmacology
quote: The second key point is that data transformation is underused. ... The need is much easier to identify than one might imagine: if the SEM increases in size in proportion to the size of the mean, the data are likely to be log‐Gaussian distributed
problem: Log-normal data (spread proportional to mean) are analysed untransformed
need: Detect SD proportional to mean across groups and suggest log transformation or lognormal tests, plotting on a log axis

role: peer-reviewed editorial with compliance audit, pharmacology
quote: It is possible to define an outlier in a control population, but only if a large number of control values are available for evaluation.
problem: Outliers are removed from small groups where they cannot be reliably identified
need: Do not offer automatic outlier removal for small n; require a pre-declared rule and report exclusions

role: peer-reviewed editorial, pharmacology
quote: As an example, one systematic review of reports of studies investigating acute lung injury revealed that, of the items expected for ARRIVE compliance, only 45% of those advised for inclusion in the Methods, and only 29% of those for inclusion in the Results section, were present
problem: ARRIVE items are largely missing from methods and results despite journal endorsement
need: Generate ARRIVE-style methods/results fragments (n per group, exclusions, statistical methods) from the analysis

role: peer-reviewed reporting guideline, animal research
quote: However, despite this level of support, recent studies have shown that important information as set out in the ARRIVE guidelines is still missing from most publications sampled. This includes details on randomisation (reported in only 30%–40% of publications), blinding (reported in only approximately 20% of publications)
problem: Randomisation and blinding are rarely reported in animal research
need: Offer a built-in randomisation/blinding step whose record is exported with the data and methods text

role: peer-reviewed reporting guideline, animal research
quote: sample size justification (reported in less than 10% of publications), and animal characteristics (all basic characteristics reported in less than 10% of publications)
problem: Sample sizes are almost never justified
need: Provide an a priori power/sample-size calculator whose output is saved with the project and cited in methods

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (271 animal studies), biomedical research
quote: Random allocation of animals to experimental groups was reported in 12% of all 271 studies in the sample
problem: Random allocation of animals is rarely reported (or done)
need: Generate random allocation lists for animals/samples inside the tool and keep the allocation with the dataset

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (271 animal studies), biomedical research
quote: Further analysis showed that overall only 70% (174/247) of papers that used a statistical method described the method employed, and also presented the numerical results with a measure of variation
problem: Statistical method and a measure of variation are not both reported in ~30% of papers
need: Every result output pairs the named test with a measure of variation and n

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (271 animal studies), biomedical research
quote: The experimental unit (e.g. a single animal or a group of animals) was not clearly identified in 13% of the 48 studies assessed in more detail
problem: The experimental unit is not identified
need: Ask the user to name the experimental unit when entering data and print it in methods/legends

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (NPQIP collaboration), life sciences
quote: For NPG in vitro studies, the proportion reaching full compliance with the Landis 4 criteria was 0% (0/159) before and 3.3% (6/176) after
problem: In vitro studies almost never report randomisation, blinding, exclusions and sample size calculation, even after a checklist
need: Provide in vitro design fields (randomised plate/well allocation, blinding, exclusions, n rationale) that populate the methods text

role: peer-reviewed meta-research (NPQIP collaboration), life sciences
quote: The proportion of studies reporting an a priori sample size calculation increased from 2.0% to 14.8%
problem: A priori sample size calculations are rarely reported
need: Built-in power analysis linked to the planned test, saved with the project

role: peer-reviewed meta-research, in vivo research
quote: Overall, 148 publications reported randomisation, of 1,028 in which this would have been appropriate (14.4%); 201 of 1,165 reported blinding (17.3%); 101 of 1,169 reported inclusion or exclusion criteria or both (10.4%); and 16 of 1,168 reported a sample size calculation (1.4%).
problem: Leading institutions' in vivo papers rarely report randomisation, blinding, exclusion criteria or sample size calculation
need: Embed randomisation, blinding, exclusion and power steps in the workflow so the information exists to report

role: peer-reviewed meta-research, in vivo research
workflow: animal research in critical care journals
quote: while some mention of randomisation was present in 47 of 77 publications (61%), the method of randomisation was described in only 1 (3%).
problem: 'Randomised' is claimed without describing how

role: peer-reviewed methods critique, Western blot quantification
